rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Layl is a singular with no attested plural; layālī is plural of layla, though some analogize it as a plural of layl or posit an underlying layāh.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أنه مفرد ولا يحفظ له جمع، ولذلك خطأ الناس من زعم أن الليالي جمع ليل، بل الليالي جمع ليلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse of poetry attests layl as a singular, while the diminutive layīla supports the analysis; layālī is an unusual plural like kayka/kayāk.
rows.anchor: ويدل على ذلك تصغيرهم لها على لييلة ونظير ليلة وليال كيكة وكياك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse glosses layālī through a poet's form laylāh; the source leaves the poet unnamed.
rows.anchor: في كل يوم وبكل ليلاه

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: In legal usage, nahār runs from dawnbreak until sunset.
rows.anchor: وأما النهار فقال الراغب: " هو في الشرع لما بين طلوع الفجر إلى غروب الشمس "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent lexical sense starts at the first lightening of dawn; Thaʿlab and al-Naḍr instead define day as beginning at sunrise, and al-Naḍr excludes the earlier time.
rows.anchor: وقال ثعلب والنضر بن شميل: " هو من طلوع الشمس " زاد النضر " ولا يعد من قبل ذلك من النهار "

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj locates the start of day at the sun's spreading light.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: " أول النهار درور الشمس "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nahār has plurals nahr and anhura, supported by usage and verse; the reported view that it has no plural treats it as a verbal noun, but the author affirms the plurals.
rows.anchor: ويجمع على نهر وأنهرة نحو قذال وقذل وأقذلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A cited line contrasts a night meal with a day meal and witnesses nahr as a form for daytime.
rows.anchor: ويجمع على نهر وأنهرة نحو قذال وقذل وأقذلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The root of nahār denotes breadth or expansion, reflected in the expanse of daylight and Q 2:25.
rows.anchor: وأنها تدل على الاتساع، ومنه: " النهار " لاتساع ضوئه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ikhtilāf is a verbal noun whose genitive is its agent: night and day each succeeds the other, as in Q 25:62 and the cited poetry.
rows.anchor: والاختلاف مصدر مضاف لفاعله، المراد باختلافهما أن كل واحد يخلف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zuhayr's line uses khalfa for alternating succession, with gazelles and their young following one another.
rows.anchor: بها العين والآرام يمشين خلفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night precedes day in the verse because it comes first; Q 36:37 supports this ordering, which the author calls the sounder view.
rows.anchor: وقدم الليل على النهار لأنه سابقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alternative says light precedes darkness; on that view the night belongs to the preceding day, whereas on the preferred view it belongs to the following day, affecting how the Day of ʿArafa is classified.
rows.anchor: وقيل: النور سابق الظلمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-fulk coordinates with the genitive khalaq governed by fī, not with al-samāwāt in an iḍāfa.
rows.anchor: عطف على " خلق " المجرور ب " في " لا على " السماوات " المجرورة بالإضافة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fulk can be singular, as in Q 26:119, or plural, as in Q 10:22.
rows.anchor: والفلك [يكون واحدا كقوله:

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: For plural fulk, Sībawayh's preferred account is a broken plural whose vowel change is only estimated; the author calls this correct.
rows.anchor: قول سيبويه - وهو الصحيح - " أنه جمع تكسير "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh infers that fulk is not a shared singular/plural form because speakers form its dual fulkān, unlike shared-form junb and shalal; hījān and dilāṣ show how vowel patterns may differ by number.
rows.anchor: فلما ثنوه وقالوا: " فلكان " علمنا أنهم لم يقصدوا الاشتراك الذي قصدوه في جنب وشلل

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash analyzes plural fulk as a collective noun, like ṣaḥb and rakb.
rows.anchor: مذهب الأخفش أنه اسم جمع كصحب وركب

rows.speaker: الشيخ
rows.claim: The Shaykh regards fulk as shared by singular and plural; the author rejects this on the evidence of its dual form and notes no rationale was offered.
rows.anchor: واختار الشيخ أنه مشترك بين الواحد والجمع، وهو محجوج بما تقدم من التثنية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When singular, fulk is masculine; feminine agreement in the verse does not prove feminine singular usage because the word may be plural.
rows.anchor: وإذا أفرد " فلك " فهو مذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fulk derives from rotation, as in the celestial sphere and a spindle whorl; the verb describes a girl's breast becoming rounded.
rows.anchor: وأصله: من الدوران ومنه: " فلك السماء " لدوران النجوم فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The present verb tajrī conveys ongoing renewal; attributing running to ships is figurative, and 'in the sea' is explanatory emphasis, like 'flies with its wings' in Q 6:38.
rows.anchor: وجاء بصلة " التي " فعلا مضارعا ليدل على التجدد والحدوث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In bi-mā yanfaʿ, mā may be a relative noun and bi marks accompaniment, or a particle with bi marking cause: ships sail for people's benefit in trade and other things.
rows.anchor: أحدهما: أنها موصولة اسمية، وعلى هذا الباء للحال أي: تجري مصحوبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the second parsing, mā is a particle and bi expresses the cause of sailing, namely people's benefit through trade and other uses.
rows.anchor: الثاني: أنها حرفية، وعلى هذا تكون الباء للسبب أي: تجري بسبب نفع الناس في التجارة وغيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first min in min al-samāʾ marks origin; the second may explain the material, mark partitive selection, or with its phrase serve as an appositive to min al-samāʾ, repeating its governor.
rows.anchor: من الأولى معناها ابتداء الغاية أي: أنزل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both prepositional phrases attach to anzala; two identical prepositions may share a governor when their meanings differ or when the second phrase is an appositive.
rows.anchor: وكلاهما أعني - من الأولى ومن الثانية - متعلقان بأنزل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The restriction against two same-form prepositions under one governor applies only when they share meaning without coordination or apposition; the verse avoids that problem.
rows.anchor: الممنوع من ذلك أن يتحدا معنى من غير عطف ولا بدل، لا تقول:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the first min can modify an omitted circumstantial expression for the relative mā itself or for the object pronoun in anzalahu: what God sent down while it was from heaven.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن تتعلق " من " الأولى بمحذوف على أنها حال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fa-aḥyā coordinates with anzala and its immediate-result fāʾ signals rapid growth; bi-hi may mark cause or instrument, figuratively, and the pronoun refers to the relative mā.
rows.anchor: عطف " أحيا " على " أنزل " الذي هو صلة بفاء التعقيب دلالة على سرعة النبات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Batha most clearly coordinates with anzala inside the relative clause; because aḥyā already coordinates with anzala, the two verbs together function as one unit.
rows.anchor: أظهرهما: أنه عطف على " أنزل " داخل تحت حكم الصلة؛ لأن قوله " فأحيا " عطف على " أنزل "

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains that the clause means God sent water into the earth and spread creatures there, which grow through fertility and live through life-giving abundance.
rows.anchor: وما أنزل في الأرض من ماء وبث فيها من كل دابة لأنهم ينمون بالخصب ويعيشون بالحيا. هذا نص الزمخشري.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative attaches batha to aḥyā, but the Shaykh objects that this relative clause then lacks a linking pronoun unless one is supplied as bi-hi.
rows.anchor: واستشكل الشيخ عطفه عليها، لأنها صلة للموصول فلا بد من ضمير يرجع من هذه الجملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Deleting a prepositional pronoun is normally allowed only under stated matching, attachment, nonrestriction, and linking conditions; those conditions fail here because the relative is not governed by the same preposition.
rows.anchor: لا يجوز حذف الضمير المجرور بحرف إلا بشروط: أن يكون الموصول مجرورا بمثل ذلك الحرف

rows.speaker: الشيخ
rows.claim: To avoid the missing-link problem, the Shaykh proposes deleting a nominal relative pronoun, a common construction he says the Basrans disallow, and cites poetry and Q 29:46 and 4:136.
rows.anchor: خرج الآية على حذف موصول اسمي، قال: " وهو جائز شائع في كلامهم، وإن كان البصريون لا يجيزونه

rows.speaker: الشيخ
rows.claim: The Shaykh also allows the first analysis despite the missing-pronoun condition, adducing poetic examples with an understood prepositional complement.
rows.anchor: وقد جاء ذلك في أشعارهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min kulli dābbah has three parses: kull is batha's object with partitive min; min is extra per al-Akhfash and kull the object; or the phrase is a circumstantial complement of an omitted object after a deleted relative, with min explanatory or partitive.
rows.anchor: يجوز في " كل " ثلاثة أوجه؛ أحدها: أن يكون في موضع المفعول به

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ posits an omitted object such as 'creatures of every kind'; the author finds this unhelpful because it makes min kulli dābbah merely its adjective.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو البقاء: " ومفعول " بث " محذوف " تقديره: وبث فيها دواب كل دابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bath is spreading and dispersal; its present is normally yabuṯṯu, though the kasra form is also attested for doubled transitive verbs, as in namma al-ḥadīth.
rows.anchor: والبث: نشر وتفريق، قال:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dābbah denotes any animal, including birds; the restriction excluding birds is refuted by verses from ʿAlqama and al-Aʿshā and by Q 24:45, which then divides creatures by their modes of walking.
rows.anchor: والدابة: اسم لكل حيوان، وزعم بعضهم إخراج الطير منه ورد عليه بقول علقمة:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAlqama's simile describes birds as moving with a creeping gait, showing that birds count as dābbah.
rows.anchor: كأنهم صابت عليهم سحابة صواعقها لطيرهن دبيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Aʿshā's line compares the movement of partridges to creeping, further supporting inclusion of birds among dābbah.
rows.anchor: دبيب قطا البطحاء في كل منهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taṣrīf means turning and alternation; its iḍāfa may make the winds the agent and omit the object (clouds), or make them the object and omit the agent (God).
rows.anchor: قوله: { وتصريف الرياح } " تصريف " مصدر صرف وهو الرد والتقليب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Riyāḥ is a broken plural whose yāʾ comes from wāw in rīḥ; phonological conditions convert wāw to yāʾ, but it returns in arwāḥ when those conditions are absent.
rows.anchor: والرياح: جمع ريح جمع تكسير، وياء الريح والرياح عن واو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Two cited poetic lines use arwāḥ, evidencing the restored wāw in the plural of rīḥ.
rows.anchor: ولذلك لما زال موجب قلبها رجعت إلى أصلها فقالوا: أرواح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥātim corrected ʿUmārah b. ʿUqayl's poetic al-aryāḥ as impermissible; the poet accepted the correction after citing riyāḥ.
rows.anchor: أبو حاتم: " إن الأرياح لا تجوز " فقال له عمارة

rows.speaker: الشيخ
rows.claim: The Shaykh recalls that al-aryāḥ occurs in poetry by authoritative Arabs, apparently modeled on the singular despite the missing sound-change trigger, like ʿīd/ aʿyād.
rows.anchor: قال الشيخ: " وفي محفوظي قديما أن " الأرياح " جاء في شعر بعض فصحاء العرب المستشهد بكلامهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author supports retaining yāʾ in al-aryāḥ to distinguish winds from arwāḥ, just as aʿyād distinguishes feast-days from sticks (aʿwād); the diminutive is also ʿuyayd.
rows.anchor: قلت: ويؤيد ما قاله الشيخ أن التزامهم الياء في الأرياح لأجل اللبس

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah says the Qurʾān usually uses the plural with mercy and singular with punishment, with an exception at Q 10:22; a report asks God for winds in plural, not a singular wind.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: " وجاءت في القرآن مجموعة مع الرحمة مفردة مع العذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects Ibn ʿAṭiyyah's formulation because readings vary at eleven places; more precisely, no plural occurs with punishment, while singular occurs with both, explaining the prophetic preference for plural in the supplication.
rows.anchor: وهذا الذي قاله يرده اختلاف القراء في أحد عشر موضعا يأتي تفصيلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At this locus Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read al-rīḥ singular, while the rest read plural: plural signals kinds such as southerly, westerly, and easterly winds; singular means the generic kind.
rows.anchor: وقرأ هنا " الريح " بالإفراد حمزة والكسائي، والباقون بالجمع

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Cloud (saḥāb) is a collective noun with singular saḥābah; Abū ʿAlī derives it from sliding or gliding, like ḥabī from crawling.
rows.anchor: سمي بذلك لانسحابه، كما قيل له: حبي لأنه يحبو، ذكر ذلك أبو علي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As a collective noun, saḥāb takes masculine singular agreement in al-musakhkhar (Q 54:20), plural agreement in Q 7:57, and can take feminine singular agreement in Q 69:7; collective nouns allow agreement by form or meaning.
rows.anchor: وباعتبار كونه اسم جنس وصفه بوصف الواحد المذكر في قوله: " المسخر "

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Taskhīr is subduing an object and making it obedient; al-Rāghib says compelling it to act is stronger than coercion.
rows.anchor: وقال الراغب: " هو القهر على الفعل وهو أبلغ من الإكراه "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bayna al-samāʾ can be governed by al-musakhkhar as the location of subjection, or be a circumstantial phrase from the passive participle's hidden pronoun, with an omitted 'being'.
rows.anchor: في " بين " قولان، أحدهما: أنه منصوب بقوله: " المسخر "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Li-āyāt is the predicate of inna placed before its delayed subject; the lām marks that postponement, and li-qawmin is an adjectival phrase for āyāt while yaʿqilūn is an adjective clause for qawm.
rows.anchor: و " لآيات " اسم إن والجار خبر مقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laylata al-ṣiyām is an accusative adverb; its governor may be aḥilla (the common parsing, rejected because permission already existed), an implied verb from rafath, or rafath itself under an expansive view of adverbs.
rows.anchor: منصوب على الظرف، وفي الناصب له ثلاثة أقوال، أحدها: - وهو المشهور عند المعربين - أنه " أحل "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preferred repair is an implied verb, 'that you engage in rafath'; rafath itself cannot govern the preceding temporal phrase because a complement of a relative clause cannot precede its relative, so the poet's duplicated verbal noun illustrates the ellipsis.
rows.anchor: الثاني: أنه مقدر مدلول عليه بلفظ " الرفث "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third analysis attaches the night phrase to rafath based on grammarians who allow temporal expansion with adverbs and prepositional phrases.
rows.anchor: الثالث: أنه متعلق بالرفث، وذلك على رأي من يرى الاتساع في الظروف والمجرورات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The iḍāfa of the night to fasting is licensed by loose association: the required intention is present at night, though fasting itself does not occur then.
rows.anchor: وأضيفت الليلة اتساعا لأن شرط صحته وهو النية موجودة فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read uḥilla passively, with God understood as agent; the active reading either omits 'God' or shifts to God's first-person voice, continuing the shift in lakum from third-person imperatives.
rows.anchor: والجمهور على " أحل " مبنيا للمفعول للعلم به وهو الله تعالى، وقرىء مبنيا للفاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rafath is followed by ilā because it is construed with the sense of ifḍāʾ, intimate approach: permission is for approaching wives through rafath.
rows.anchor: وعدي " الرفث " بإلى، وإنما يتعدى بالباء لما ضمن من معنى الإفضاء

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh's reading is al-rafūth rather than al-rafath.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عبد الله " الرفوث "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rafath lexically means indecent speech: it is the verbal noun of rafiṯa, while arfatha means to engage in such speech; al-ʿAjjāj provides a poetic usage.
rows.anchor: والرفث لغة مصدر: رفث يرفث إذا تكلم بالفحش

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj, transmitting from Ibn ʿAbbās, calls rafath a comprehensive expression for everything a man desires from a woman.
rows.anchor: وقال الزجاج: - ويروى عن ابن عباس - " إن الرفث كلمة جامعة لكل ما يريده الرجل من المرأة "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A view takes rafath as sexual intercourse itself, supported by two poetic examples; the author says these do not prove it because they may refer to preliminaries such as caressing or kissing.
rows.anchor: ولهن عن رفث الرجال نفار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: While in consecration, Ibn ʿAbbās recited a flirtatious verse about women and asked whether the birds' omen proved it; when told he had committed rafath, he answered that rafath is only with women.
rows.anchor: وأنشد ابن عباس وهو محرم:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kuntum takhtānūna is the predicate of inna, and takhtānūna is the predicate of kāna.
rows.anchor: قوله: { كنتم تختانون } في محل رفع خبر لأن.

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ reads kāna as past in both form and meaning, describing actual past lapses followed by repentance; the author objects to his alternative future reading expressed through narrative kāna.
rows.anchor: قال أبو البقاء: " وكنتم هنا لفظها لفظ الماضي ومعناها المضي أيضا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Takhtānūna is from iftiʿāl of khiyānah, whose root has wāw, as shown by khāna/yakhūnu and khūn/khiyānah; zuhayr uses khānah in a line about a mount's back.
rows.anchor: و " تختانون " تفتعلون من الخيانة، وعين الخيانة واو

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī treats ikhtiyān like iktisāb: the added form conveys greater intensity than the base khiyānah, consistent with added form suggesting added meaning.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: " والاختيان: من الخيانة كالاكتساب من الكسب، فيه زيادة وشدة "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further gloss takes takhtānūna anfusakum as looking after or attending to yourselves through intercourse; takhawwanahu and takhawwalahu both mean to tend, with nūn substituted for the more common lām.
rows.anchor: وقيل هنا: تختانون أنفسكم أي: تتعهدونها بإتيان النساء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If ʿalima means 'knew' and takes one object, anna and its clause fill it; if it takes two, the clause fills both for Sībawayh but only one for al-Akhfash, with the other omitted.
rows.anchor: و " علم " إن كانت المتعدية لواحد بمعنى عرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hun(n)a libāsun lakum is an independent explanatory statement rather than a syntactically governed clause; putting it first highlights men's need for women and their initiating the relationship.
rows.anchor: لا محل له من الإعراب، لأنه بيان للإحلال فهو استئناف وتفسير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The garment metaphor means close intimacy; al-Nābighah al-Jaʿdī's poem describes a lover embracing a woman until she becomes like clothing to him.
rows.anchor: كقوله - هو النابغة الجعدي -:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ān ordinarily means the present, though it can denote nearby past or future; Abū al-Baqāʾ takes it here as the formerly prohibited time, now near enough to count as present.
rows.anchor: " والآن: حقيقته الوقت الذي أنت فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the phrase means 'now We have permitted you intimacy'; the imperative implies an omitted perfect verb and al-ān keeps its ordinary present sense.
rows.anchor: وقيل: هذا كلام محمول على معناه، والتقدير: فالآن قد أبحنا لكم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A reading wa-ittabiʿū is transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, Muʿāwiyah b. Qurrah, and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī; they gloss 'what God prescribed' as Laylat al-Qadr and following its reward.
rows.anchor: وقرىء: " واتبعوا " من الاتباع، وتروى عن ابن عباس ومعاوية ابن قرة والحسن البصري

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī calls the Laylat al-Qadr interpretation close to an innovation in exegesis.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: " وهو قريب من بدع التفاسير "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥattā marks the endpoint of eating and drinking; min al-khayṭ is an ablative of starting point governed by yatabayyana, understood as distinguishing the white thread from the black.
rows.anchor: " حتى " هنا غاية لقوله: " كلوا واشربوا " بمعنى إلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min al-fajr may be partitive and attach to yatabayyana, or be a circumstantial phrase from al-abyaḍ with min explaining the kind; treating it as a specification is rejected.
rows.anchor: و " من الفجر " يجوز فيه ثلاثة أوجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse omits 'from the night' after the black thread because that is understood from the white thread; dawn alone anchors the legal rules on intimacy, food, and drink.
rows.anchor: لأنه هو المنوط به الأحكام المذكورة من المباشرة والأكل والشرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image compares daylight to a white thread and night to a black one. It is an unusually forceful simile, called a kind of metaphor because the comparison term is folded into the image, though the phrase 'from dawn' makes the referent explicit.
rows.anchor: وهذا من أحسن التشبيهات حيث شبه بياض النهار بخيط أبيض، وسواد الليل بخيط أسود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When ʿAdī b. Ḥātim understood the threads literally, the Prophet replied that his pillow must be broad (another report says his nape was broad); another Companion reportedly made the same mistake.
rows.anchor: حتى إنه لما ذكر عدي بن حاتم لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إنه فهم من الآية حقيقة الخيط تعجب منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the clarification 'from dawn' came a full year after 'the white thread' and 'the black thread'; some Companions had meanwhile taken the image literally.
rows.anchor: ويروى أن بين قوله " الخيط الأبيض " " من الخيط الأسود " عاما كاملا في النزول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author explains why the expression is ultimately a simile rather than an unmarked metaphor: a metaphor needs contextual evidence, whereas the explicit dawn phrase supplies the comparison and some Companions read literally before it was added.
rows.anchor: لأن الاستعارة لا بد فيها من دلالة حالية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fajr is the verbal noun of fajara/yafjuru, meaning to split or break open.
rows.anchor: والفجر مصدر فجر يفجر أي: انشق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ilā al-layl either marks the endpoint of completing the fast or is a circumstantial phrase; because night is outside the day, ilā does not include it.
rows.anchor: قوله: { إلى الليل } فيه وجهان: أحدهما: أنه متعلق بالإتمام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wa-antum ʿākifūn is circumstantial of the subject of 'do not approach'; the prohibition applies while one has undertaken mosque retreat, while intercourse in a mosque is forbidden even without retreat.
rows.anchor: " وأنتم عاكفون " جملة حالية من فاعل " تباشروهن "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿUkūf is staying and remaining; the verb has both yaʿkufu and yaʿkifu forms, illustrated by readings of Q 7:138 and poetry by al-Farazdaq and al-Ṭirimmāḥ.
rows.anchor: والعكوف: الإقامة والملازمة له، يقال: عكف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source says iftiʿāl is used for the good and inﬁʿāl for the bad; legal iʿtikāf is a defined form of residence with conditions, analogous to the legal reality of prayer.
rows.anchor: ويقال: الافتعال منه في الخير، والانفعال في الشر.

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatādah reads ʿakifūn, paralleling the forms ʿākif/ʿakif and bār/ barr.
rows.anchor: وقرأ قتادة: " عكفون " كأنه يقال: عاكف وعكف نحو بار وبر

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash reads 'in the mosque' in the singular, apparently intending the generic institution.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش: " في المسجد " بالإفراد كأنه يريد الجنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tilka ḥudūd Allāh cannot refer only to the single intercourse prohibition; it encompasses the whole fasting passage's commands and prohibitions, with the plural limits reflecting their combined force.
rows.anchor: واسم الإشارة أخبر عنه بجمع، فلا جائز أن يشار به إلى ما نهي عنه في الاعتكاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because a commanded act cannot be what 'do not approach them' prohibits, the plural limits include implied prohibitions generated by the preceding commands as well as the explicit final prohibition.
rows.anchor: والأمر بالشيء نهي عن ضده، فبهذا الاعتبار كانت عدة مناهي

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ supplies an omitted warning before the fāʾ; the author rejects treating fāʾ as extra, since that would require the following phrase to be accusative by the more idiomatic interlocking construction, contrary to the unanimous raised reading.
rows.anchor: قال أبو البقاء: " دخول الفاء هنا عاطفة على شيء محذوف تقديره: " تنبهوا فلا تقربوها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥudūd means prevention and a boundary's endpoint; ḥaddād is a gatekeeper because he prevents passage, and a valid definition both excludes outsiders and includes what belongs within.
rows.anchor: والحدود: جمع حد وهو المنع، ومنه قيل للبواب: حداد، لأنه يمنع من العبور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A ban on approaching is stronger than a ban on touching or mixing with the prohibited matter.
rows.anchor: والنهي عن القربان أبلغ من النهي عن الالتباس بالشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This passage says 'do not approach' because an explicit prohibition immediately precedes it; Q 2:229 and 4:14 say 'do not transgress' after legal rulings, where crossing the prescribed limit is apt.
rows.anchor: عقب بيان أحكام ذكرت قبل كالطلاق والعدة والإيلاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kāf in kadhālika is accusative either as an adjective or circumstantial modifier of an omitted verbal noun meaning 'a clarification like this'; the latter reflects Sībawayh's view.
rows.anchor: الكاف في محل نصب: إما نعتا لمصدر محذوف، أي: بيانا مثل هذا البيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most read aw with a quiescent wāw as a division between examples; another view makes it a choice between wonders. Abū Sufyān b. Ḥusayn reads a fatḥa, parsing a conjunction wāw preceded by an interrogative hamza.
rows.anchor: الجمهور على سكون واو " أو " وهي هنا للتفصيل، وقيل: للتخيير بين التعجب

rows.speaker: الكسائي والفراء
rows.claim: One parse coordinates ka-alladhī by sense with alam tara, yielding 'Have you seen the one who disputed Abraham, or the one who passed a town?'; such semantic coordination is attested in poetry but grammarians say it is not analogically productive.
rows.anchor: وتقديره عند الكسائي والفراء: هل رأيت كالذي حاج إبراهيم أو كالذي مر على قرية

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: A second, strong parse supplies an omitted raʾayta, cued by alam tara; both clauses then express wonder, and the author favors this over semantic coordination because ellipsis is common.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: " أو كالذي: معناه أو رأيت مثل الذي "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third analysis treats the kāf as extra, as in Q 42:11 and a poetic example; it is weak because words should not be assumed extra without need.
rows.anchor: الثالث: أن الكاف زائدة كهي في قوله: ليس كمثله شيء

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash treats kāf as a noun meaning 'like'; the author calls this correct by the evidence, construing the phrase as 'or the like of the one who passed', though most Basrans disagree.
rows.anchor: والرابع: أن الكاف اسم بمعنى مثل، لا حرف، وهو مذهب الأخفش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Evidence for nominal kāf includes its parallel use with mithl as a subject in poetry and its ability to take prepositions and serve as their complement.
rows.anchor: ومنها دخول حروف الجر، والإسناد إليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause wa-hiya khāwiyah has five proposed functions: circumstantial of the passer; circumstantial of the town (if 'on its roofs' modifies it or a bare indefinite can take a circumstantial); circumstantial of its roofs, fronted; or of the possessive pronoun in 'its roofs'.
rows.anchor: هذه الجملة فيها/ خمسة أوجه، أحدها أن تكون حالا من فاعل " مر "

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ allows the circumstantial to come from the pronoun attached to ʿurūsh, with the relation of possession as governor; the author calls this weak but eased by the roofs being part of the town.
rows.anchor: قال أبو البقاء: " والعامل معنى الإضافة وهو ضعيف مع جوازه "

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: A fifth option makes wa-hiya khāwiyah an adjective of qaryah, although the author notes the usual objection that wāw does not separate adjective and noun; al-Zamakhsharī explains it as emphasizing attachment, following Ibn Jinnī.
rows.anchor: وإن كان الزمخشري قد أجاز ذلك في قوله تعالى:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ's detailed dependencies tie the descriptive/circumstantial options to whether ʿalā ʿurūshihā is a repeated-preposition substitute for qaryah or an adjective; the author says this argument has an evident problem.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا البناء نظر لا يخفى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAlā ʿurūshihā can be a badal of qaryah with the preposition repeated, an adjective ('a town fallen upon its roofs'), a complement of khāwiyah meaning collapsed, or attached to an omitted thābit ('standing') if khāwiyah means empty of inhabitants; the author says the last is unsupported.
rows.anchor: قوله: { على عروشها } فيه أربعة أوجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some take ʿalā to mean maʿa ('with'), and ʿurūsh then means the buildings themselves.
rows.anchor: وقيل: " على " بمعنى " مع " أي: مع عروشها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khāwī means empty or vacant and has several related forms; khawāʾ may describe an empty house, hunger from an empty belly, level terrain, or a camel lifting its side from the ground.
rows.anchor: والخاوي: الخالي. يقال: خوت الدار تخوي خواء بالمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poetic line uses khawāʾ for a camel holding its side above the ground.
rows.anchor: والخوى: الجوع لخلو البطن من الزاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿUrūsh is the plural of ʿarsh, a house roof or anything built for shade; another view uses it for the building itself, supported by a line about toppling a people's structures.
rows.anchor: والعروش: جمع عرش، وهو سقف البيت، وكذلك كل ما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In annā yuhyī, annā can mean 'when' (then temporal) or 'how' (then circumstantial); the apparent sense is 'how', governed by yuhyī, as is baʿda.
rows.anchor: في " أنى " وجهان، أحدهما: أن تكون بمعنى " متى "

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ assigns annā a circumstantial position when it means 'how'.
rows.anchor: والثاني: انها بمعنى كيف. قال أبو البقاء: فيكون موضعها حالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revival and death may be figurative for rebuilding and ruin, or literal with 'the inhabitants' supplied; hadhihi may instead point to the decayed bones and scattered bodies of the townspeople.
rows.anchor: والإحياء والإماتة مجاز إن أريد بهما العمران والخراب، أو حقيقة

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ says miʾata ʿāmin is a time adverb by sense ('kept him for a hundred years'), or supplies an omitted fa-labitha; the author says both repairs are unnecessary because God made him dead for that duration.
rows.anchor: ولا حاجة إلى هذين التأويلين، بل المعنى جعله ميتا مئة عام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Miʾah is a known unit of one hundred with deleted final yāʾ, inferred from amʾaytu ('made into a hundred'); its plural is miʾāt, with the poetic form miʾūn rare.
rows.anchor: و " مئة " عقد من العدد معروف

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqāsh derives ʿām from ʿāmah/ʿāwmah, a year-long solar circuit, linking it to swimming and Q 36:40; on this account ʿām and ʿawm parallel qawl and qāl.
rows.anchor: وقال النقاش: " هو في الأصل مصدر سمي به الزمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wāw in ʿām is shown by the diminutive ʿuwaym and plural aʿwām.
rows.anchor: وعينه واو لقولهم في التصغير، عويم، وفي التكسير:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kam is an accusative time adverb governed by labithta, with an omitted specification such as 'days' or 'time'.
rows.anchor: قوله: { كم } منصوب على الظرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aw in yawman aw baʿḍa yawm most likely means bal ('rather'), not doubt; bal labithta coordinates with an omitted 'I did not stay a day or part of one'.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن " أو " في قوله: { يوما أو بعض يوم } بمعنى " بل " للإضراب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nāfiʿ, ʿĀṣim, and Ibn Kathīr pronounce the thāʾ distinctly throughout the Qurʾān; the other readers assimilate it.
rows.anchor: وقرأ نافع وعاصم وابن كثير بإظهار الثاء في جميع القرآن، والباقون بالإدغام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lam yat as a circumstantial clause is debated: some prefer wāw before imperfect negation with lam, others prefer mā or lammā; both rules are false because Qurʾān has examples with and without wāw, including Q 3:174 and 6:93.
rows.anchor: وزعم آخرون أن الأولى نفي المضارع الواقع حالا بما ولما وكلا الزعمين غير صحيحين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular pronoun in lam yatasannah after food and drink is explained because they form one nourishment, or because it refers to the nearer drink and the food clause is elided (or its nonchange follows a fortiori); a third account uses singular for dual, which the author rejects.
rows.anchor: قيل: قد تقدم شيئان وهما " طعامك وشرابك " ولم يعد الضمير إلا مفردا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī retain hāʾ at pause but drop it in connected speech; the other readers retain it in both positions. For their reading it marks pause, while the common reading may retain a pause marker in connection or have original hāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي: " لم يتسنه " بالهاء وقفا وبحذفها وصلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If yatasannah derives from sanah (year), its deleted root lām is wāw, as shown by the diminutive and plural sanīyah/sanawāt and forms such as sānaytu and asnata al-qawm.
rows.anchor: إن لامها المحذوفة واو، ولذلك ترد في التصغير والجمع

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr derives yatasannah from masnūn ('changed'), with three adjacent nūns simplified through substitution and sound change; al-Zajjāj rejects this because masnūn means molded or poured along a way.
rows.anchor: والأصل: يتسنن بثلاث نونات، فاستثقل توالي الأمثال

rows.speaker: النقاش
rows.claim: Al-Naqqāsh derives the form from asina al-māʾ ('water changed'); grammarians reject the derivation as morphologically faulty, though the sense is right, and the author offers a possible metathesis explanation.
rows.anchor: وحكي عن النقاش أنه قال: " هو مأخوذ من أسن الماء " أي تغير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hāʾ may instead be a root consonant in the Hijazi form of sanah; diminutive, plural, verb, and a poetic line support sanīhah, sanīhāt, and sānahat.
rows.anchor: أن تكون الهاء أصلا بنفسها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lam yatasannah means that the food and drink did not change through the years; this is better than Abū al-Baqāʾ's 'no years passed over it', which contradicts the stated hundred years.
rows.anchor: لم يتغير بمر السنين عليه

rows.speaker: أبي
rows.claim: Ubayy reads lam yasnah, assimilating the tāʾ into the sīn, like the assimilation in Q 37:8; Ṭalḥah b. Muṣarrif reads lamʾiata sanah.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبي: " لم يسنه " بإدغام التاء في السين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wa-li-najʿalaka may attach to an omitted verb ('We did this to make you a sign'), coordinate with an omitted purpose, or—with an extra wāw—attach to 'look at your donkey'; the author rejects claims of fronting and back-shifting among the three commands to look.
rows.anchor: فيه ثلاثة أوجه، أحدها: أنه متعلق بفعل محذوف مقدر بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām is purposive and the following verb is subjunctive with an implicit an; āyah is the second object of jaʿala in its 'make/transform' sense, and li-l-nās modifies āyah, with al either referring to the surviving townsfolk or humanity in general.
rows.anchor: وهذه اللام لام كي، والفعل بعدها منصوب بإضمار " أن "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kayfa is an accusative circumstantial expression governed by nanshizuhā, with the object pronoun as its referent; unẓur cannot govern an interrogative because it has clause-initial position.
rows.anchor: قوله: { كيف } منصوب نصب الأحوال، والعامل فيها " ننشزها "

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ takes both kayfa and the interrogative clause as a circumstantial phrase for the bones; the author rejects this because an interrogative clause cannot itself be a circumstantial, though kayfa alone can.
rows.anchor: وهذا ليس بشيء، لأن هذه جملة استفهام، والاستفهام لا يقع حالا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author instead parses the whole 'how We raise them' clause as a substitute for al-ʿiẓām, governed by the suspended visual verb; an omitted 'state of' makes the substitution grammatical, as in 'I knew Zayd: whose father is he?'.
rows.anchor: والذي يقتضيه النظر الصحيح في هذه المسألة وأمثالها أن تكون جملة " كيف ننشزها " بدلا من " العظام "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr and the Ḥijāzī readers pronounce nunshiruha with rāʾ; the remaining readers have nunshizuha with zāy, while Ibn ʿAbbās and al-Nakhaʿī transmit additional vowel and consonant variants.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو عمرو والحرميان: " ننشرها " بضم النون وكسر الشين والراء المهملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Ḥijāzī rāʾ reading derives from anshara Allāh al-mawtā ('God revived the dead'); Ibn ʿAbbās's triliteral nashara can mean the same, or spreading/unfolding as a metaphor for revival, though its usual intransitive reflexive sense cannot fit this transitive construction.
rows.anchor: فأما قراءة الحرميين: فمن " أنشر الله الموتى " بمعنى أحياهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poem uses nāshir for a dead person who has come back to life, showing intransitive nashara meaning 'to live again'.
rows.anchor: ومن مجيء " نشر " لازما قوله:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The zāy reading comes from nashz ('elevation'): the bones are moved and raised into alignment for revival.
rows.anchor: وأما قراءة الزاي فمن " النشز " وهو الارتفاع

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah objects that nushūz is gradual rising and does not naturally mean lifting bones together; he supports this sense with expressions for a camel's tooth rising and 'rise, and they rose'.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: " ويقلق عندي أن يكون النشوز رفع العظام بعضها إلى بعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With ḍamma, nunshiz is from anshaza; with fatḥa it is from nashaza, both used transitively. A yāʾ reading makes God the subject, and Ubayy reads nunshiʾuhā from nashʾah.
rows.anchor: ومن ضم النون فمن " أنشز "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some prefer zāy because bones revive by joining together, not individually; the author rejects the claim that bones cannot be alive, citing Q 36:78, and supplies the omitted reference 'the donkey's bones'.
rows.anchor: ورجح بعضهم قراءة الزاي على الراء بأن قال: العظام لا تحيا على الانفراد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laḥman is the second object of naksūhā, as with a verb of giving; clothing the bones in flesh is metaphorical, like Labīd's verse about wearing Islam as a cloak.
rows.anchor: قوله: { لحما } مفعول ثان ل " نكسوها " وهو من باب أعطى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For falammā tabayyana, one view supplies an implicit subject such as the manner in which revival became clear; the author prefers it over al-Zamakhsharī's 'what had confused him' because the context supports the former.
rows.anchor: أحدهما: مضمر يفسره سياق الكلام، تقديره: فلما تبين له كيفية الإحياء

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī analyzes tabayyana and aʿlama by syntactic attraction: anna Allāha can be the subject of the first and object of the second, with the second verb governing and the first subject omitted.
rows.anchor: يعني أن " تبين " يطلب فاعلا، و " أعلم " يطلب مفعولا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says this is the preferred Basran form of tanāzuʿ, illustrated by Q 18:96 and 69:19; he says first-verb governance would require a different object pronoun construction.
rows.anchor: فلما أعمل الثاني أضمر في الأول فاعلا، ولا يجوز أن يكون من إعمال الأول

rows.speaker: الشيخ
rows.claim: The Shaykh objects that tanāzuʿ requires the two governors to share a syntactic link; here the second verb is governed by qāla (the answer to lammā), while tabayyana is governed within the lammā clause, so the verbs do not compete for one constituent.
rows.anchor: إلا أن الشيخ رد عليه بأن شرط الإعمال على ما نص عليه النحويون اشتراك العاملين

rows.speaker: الشيخ
rows.claim: The Shaykh notes that grammarians do not analyze unlinked sequences such as 'when he came, I struck Zayd' as tanāzuʿ, and rejects al-Zamakhsharī's alleged competition between tabayyana and aʿlama.
rows.anchor: ولم يذكر النحاة التنازع في نحو: " لو جاء قتلت زيدا "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Shaykh also sees inconsistency in calling tabayyana's subject 'omitted' after calling it 'implicit'; if deletion is intended, that is al-Kisāʾī's account, since he disallows a hidden subject before its later expression.
rows.anchor: وقد ناقض قوله حيث جعل الفاعل محذوفا كما تقدم في عبارته، والحذف ينافي الإضمار

rows.speaker: الشيخ
rows.claim: The Shaykh cites poetry to debate whether an unexpressed subject can be anticipated before its later mention, adducing taʿfaqu bi-l-arṭā and the line huwīnani wa-hawaytu.
rows.anchor: فإن كان أراد بالإضمار في قوله: " وفاعل تبين مضمر " الحذف فهو قول الكسائي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reads tabayyana passively, with the following prepositional phrase as deputy subject; Ibn al-Sumayfiʿ reads ybayyanu without tāʾ, also passive, with an understood 'manner of revival' or the prepositional phrase as deputy subject.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس: " تبين " مبنيا للمفعول، والقائم مقام الفاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority read qāla actively. With Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī's imperative aʿlam ('know'), the speaker may be God or an angel addressing the passer, or the passer may address himself by treating himself as another person (tajrīd).
rows.anchor: الجمهور على " قال " مبنيا للفاعل

rows.speaker: أبو البقاء
rows.claim: Abū al-Baqāʾ calls the passer's self-address tajrīd, as if he detached a speaker from himself; several cited poems use such self-address.
rows.anchor: قال أبو البقاء: " ما تقول لنفسك: اعلم يا عبد الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the other readers' present-tense aʿlam, the passer is the subject and says, 'I know.'
rows.anchor: وأما على قراءة غيرهما: " أعلم " مضارعا للمتكلم ففاعل " قال " ضمير المار

rows.speaker: الأعمش
rows.claim: Al-Aʿmash reads qīla passively; its deputy subject may be the verbal noun or the following clause, as in an earlier discussion in the sūrah.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأعمش: " قيل " مبنيا للمفعول. والقائم مقام الفاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī have the imperative aʿlam; most others have first-person aʿlam, while al-Jaʿfī from Abū Bakr has the imperative of aʿlama. The anna clause fills both objects, or one with the other omitted, under the prior disagreement.
rows.anchor: وقرأ حمزة والكسائي: " اعلم " على الأمر، والباقون: " أعلم " مضارعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mathal is the subject and ka-mathali ḥabbah its predicate; the comparison requires an ellipsis because spenders are not themselves like a grain. Proposed omissions are the spender/their spending, the sower of a grain, or matching omissions on both sides.
rows.anchor: ولا بد من حذف حتى يصح التشبيه، لأن الذين ينفقون لا يشبهون بنفس الحبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author refers readers to his fuller analysis of Q 2:171; treating either kāf or mathal as an extra word is very remote and should be disregarded.
rows.anchor: والقول بزيادة الكاف أو " مثل " بعيد جدا، فلا يلتفت إلى قائله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḥabbah is one edible grain, most often wheat; al-Mutalammis supplies poetic evidence. With kasrah, ḥibbah means vegetable seeds not eaten as staple, while ḥubb with ḍamma means grain.
rows.anchor: والحبة: واحدة الحب، وهو ما يزرع للاقتيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Anbatat sabʿa sanābil is an adjectival clause describing ḥabbah as a grain that sprouted seven ears.
rows.anchor: هذه الجملة في محل جر لأنها صفة لحبة، كأنه قيل: كمثل حبة منبتة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, and Hishām assimilate the feminine tāʾ into the sīn of sabʿ; the others pronounce it distinctly. Near articulation and analogical alternations such as nās/nāt explain the assimilation, witnessed in verse.
rows.anchor: وأدغم تاء التأنيث في سين " سبع " أبو عمرو وحمزة والكسائي وهشام

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī asks why this verse uses the broken plural sanābil rather than the sound plural sanbilāt as in Q 12:43, and says plural patterns interchange by extension; the author finds this answer inadequate.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري: " فإن قلت: هلا قيل " سبع سنبلات "

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sound plurals quantify numbers only when no other plural exists, as with samāwāt, baqarāt, āyāt, and ṣalawāt; the rare poetic samāyā is disregarded. They can also be chosen through adjacency, as sanbilāt beside baqarāt in Q 12:43.
rows.anchor: اعلم أن جمعي السلامة لا يميز بهما عدد إلا في موضعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Without adjacency, when a noun has both sound and broken plurals the broken plural is used for counting; sound forms such as ṭarīqāt and laylāt are possible but disfavored beside seven paths or nights.
rows.anchor: ولذلك إذا لم توجد المجاورة ميز بجمع التكسير دون جمع السلامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Among competing plurals, mafaʿil broken plurals are preferred to sound plurals (e.g. three Aḥmads/Zaynabs); when the non-sound plural is uncommon, sound or common broken forms are preferred, with the rare alternatives noted.
rows.anchor: فإن كان من باب مفاعل أوثر على التصحيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sunbulah has two analyses: nūn is original because sunbala al-zarʿ means the crop produced its ear, or nūn is extra (the common view) because asbala al-zarʿ is attested; the two verb patterns resemble sabaṭ/sabaṭr.
rows.anchor: والسنبلة فيها قولان، أحدهما: أن نونها أصلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fī kulli sunbula is an adjectival phrase modifying sanābil (genitive) or sabʿ (accusative), in either case dependent on an omitted term; miʾah can be the prepositional phrase's subject or a fronted predicate with miʾah as subject.
rows.anchor: هذا الجار في محل جر صفة لسنابل، أو نصب صفة لسبع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first parse of marfūʿ miʾah, as the subject licensed by the dependent prepositional phrase, is preferable because single-word modifiers are the default; an omitted pronoun means 'in each ear of them'.
rows.anchor: لأن الأصل الوصف بالمفردات دون الجمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majority raise miʾah; a reading accusative is possible by an omitted verb ('it produced/brought forth') or as badal of sabʿ, but the author rejects the proposed whole, part, and inclusion appositions because their relations fail.
rows.anchor: والجمهور على رفع " مئة " على ما تقدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The simplest account of accusative miʾah deletes a noun: 'the grain of seven ears'; then miʾata ḥabbah is a partitive apposition to that omitted grain.
rows.anchor: وأسهل من هذا كله أن يكون ثم مضاف محذوف، أي: حب سبع سنابل
